text: More than 500 years ago, Spanish colonists began bringing enslaved people from West Africa to the island of Hispaniola.
The word Vodou comes from the Fon language of West Africa, where it meant a spirit.
src: c. 1512: Spanish colonists on Hispaniola begin importing enslaved West Africans
The word Vodou comes from the Fon language of West Africa: Vôdoun, a word for a spirit or deity in the kingdom of Dahomey

text: A French law forbade them to practise African religions openly, so they held their rites in secret, usually at night.
More than 250 years ago, their African religions mixed with Catholic ones and became Vodou.
src: The Code Noir of 1685 forbade the open practice of African religions, so rites were held in secret, usually at night
c. 1750: Among the enslaved of Saint-Domingue, African religions mixed with Catholic and Freemasonic elements take the form of Vodou

text: Vodouists believe in one God, Bondye, who is so far away that they rarely pray to him directly.
Instead they serve the lwa, spirits who are often linked to Catholic saints.
src: Vodou teaches that there is one supreme God, Bondye / so remote that Vodouists see little point in approaching him directly
Vodouists serve Bondye, a remote creator God, through the lwa / most are linked to Catholic saints

text: At night ceremonies of drums, songs and dancing, believers invite a lwa to come and speak through a worshipper.
Designs called vèvè are drawn on the temple floor in cornmeal to call the lwa.
src: In the dans, the night ceremony of drumming, song and dance, a lwa is invited to possess a worshipper, the chwal or “horse”, and to speak through them to the congregation
the vèvè, designs drawn in cornmeal, ash or coffee grounds on the temple floor to summon the lwa

text: Vodou became Haiti’s main faith after the Haitian Revolution, though outsiders long mocked it as sorcery.
Today most Haitians practise both Vodou and Catholicism, and Haitians have carried it to many other countries.
src: Forbidden in the colony, Vodou became Haiti’s dominant religion after the Revolution; long maligned by outsiders as sorcery
Most Haitians practise both Vodou and Catholicism / has spread with Haitian emigrants
